paper_a.title: Robust Stochastic Approximation Approach to Stochastic Programming

paper_b.title: Stochastic First- and Zeroth-order Methods for Nonconvex Stochastic Programming

metadata.description: Ghadimi-Lan (paper B) extends the classical/robust SA framework of Nemirovski-Juditsky-Lan-Shapiro (paper A) from the convex setting to nonconvex smooth stochastic optimization. The key extension: paper A obtains O(1/sqrt(N)) rates on the optimality gap E[f(x_avg)-f*] under convexity using projection/mirror-descent and iterate averaging, while paper B obtains analogous O(1/sqrt(N)) rates on the expected squared gradient norm E||grad f(x_R)||^2 by using a randomly-indexed iterate (RSG) instead of averaging, and further extends the framework to derivative-free (zeroth-order) settings via Gaussian smoothing. Both papers share the Juditsky-Nemirovski martingale large-deviation lemma and parallel two-phase / averaging meta-strategies for high-probability bounds.

matches.explanation: Both papers state the canonical stochastic optimization problem min E[F(x,xi)]. Paper A constrains x to a bounded closed convex set X and assumes f convex (and possibly strongly convex); paper B drops the constraint set (x in R^n) and crucially drops convexity, requiring only L-smoothness and bounded-below f. This is the central problem-level extension: nonconvex smooth replaces convex (constrained).

Paper B's simulation-based / zeroth-order variant of the stochastic programming problem mirrors paper A's setup but with only function-value (zeroth-order) noisy access. Paper A only ever uses first-order (subgradient) oracles, so this is a derivative-free extension of the classical SA setting.

Paper A's (A1) iid sampling oracle plus (A2) stochastic subgradient oracle (with E[G]=g in subdifferential of f) correspond to paper B's A1 unbiased bounded-variance stochastic gradient assumption (E[G]=grad f, E||G-grad f||^2 <= sigma^2). Paper B sharpens to a smooth setting (true gradient, not subgradient) and explicitly bounds variance rather than the second moment of G.

Paper B's A2 (sub-Gaussian/light-tail tail condition on the gradient noise) does not have a paper-original analogue in paper A's assumption list per se; paper A states an analogous light-tail condition inline (e.g. (2.50), (3.16)) used in its large-deviation propositions, but it is not extracted as a standalone Assumption node in paper A.
Paper B's A3 (unbiased stochastic function values for the zeroth-order oracle) has no counterpart in paper A, which is purely first-order.

The (epsilon, Lambda)-solution definition (Prob{||grad f||^2 <= epsilon} >= 1-Lambda) is paper B's specifically nonconvex performance criterion. Paper A reports E[f(x)-f*] (convex) and large-deviation tails on f(x)-f*, but never on gradient norm; this is a paper-B-specific criterion arising from the nonconvex setting.

Gaussian smoothing of f and the corresponding finite-difference gradient estimator have no analogue in paper A (no zeroth-order machinery). These are external (Nesterov 2011) constructions that paper B brings in to extend SA to derivative-free.

Paper A's bounded-second-moment condition E||G(x,xi)||_2^2 <= M^2 (eq. (2.5)) plays the same role as the variance bound in paper B's A1 (E||G-grad f||^2 <= sigma^2). Paper B centers the noise (variance), whereas paper A bounds the raw second moment of G; in the convex bounded-X setting these are essentially interchangeable.

Paper B's smoothness inequality (descent lemma) and convex co-coercivity bound are foundational tools cited from Nesterov for the nonconvex/smooth analysis. Paper A operates in a (sub)gradient/non-smooth setting and uses the prox-mapping inequality (LP247.1) instead; no direct counterpart.

Both are SGD-style stochastic approximation methods: paper A's classical SA is x_{j+1} = Pi_X(x_j - gamma_j G(x_j,xi_j)) (projected SGD); paper B's RSG is x_{k+1} = x_k - gamma_k G(x_k,xi_k) (unconstrained SGD) with the addition of returning a randomly-indexed iterate x_R rather than the last iterate. The randomized return is the key new ingredient enabling nonconvex analysis.

Paper A's robust E-SA with averaging and paper B's RSG share the same goal: robustify the classical SA recurrence so that O(1/sqrt(N)) rates hold without needing strong convexity / fine-tuned stepsize. They differ in the meta-strategy: paper A uses constant stepsizes plus weighted averaging of iterates; paper B uses constant stepsizes plus random selection of an iterate. Both reduce sensitivity to stepsize misspecification.

Paper B's two-phase 2-RSG (run RSG S times, post-select the best by ||g(x_s)||) is a high-probability boosting wrapper analogous in spirit to paper A's averaging-based robustness, but the mechanism differs (post-optimization selection from independent runs vs. weighted averaging within one run). Both are paper-original constructions targeting the same goal of robust low-failure-probability convergence.

Paper A's mirror descent SA (prox-mapping based on a distance-generating function adapted to the geometry of X) has no counterpart in paper B, which works in unconstrained Euclidean R^n. This is paper A's central methodological contribution beyond classical SA, orthogonal to paper B's nonconvex extension.
Paper A's saddle-point mirror SA (for stochastic convex-concave saddle problems) has no paper B counterpart. Paper B is single-objective minimization.
RSGF (zeroth-order randomized stochastic gradient-free method) has no analogue in paper A. This is paper B's derivative-free extension.
2-RSGF (two-phase zeroth-order method) has no analogue in paper A; paper-B-specific.

Paper A's Theorem on O(t^{-1}) convergence of classical SA under strong convexity establishes E||x_j-x_*||^2 = O(1/j); paper B's Theorem 1 (RSG convergence) establishes (1/L)E||grad f(x_R)||^2 <= (D_f^2 + sigma^2 sum gamma_k^2)/sum(2 gamma_k - L gamma_k^2). These are the core single-run convergence theorems on each side: same algorithmic backbone (SGD recurrence), but paper A measures iterate distance to optimum under strong convexity, while paper B measures expected squared gradient norm under nonconvex smoothness. Direct extension across the convex-nonconvex divide.

Paper A's Theorem 2 (O(N^{-1/2}) efficiency of robust E-SA with constant stepsize gamma_t = theta D_X /(M sqrt(N))) and paper B's Corollary 1 (constant-stepsize RSG bound L D_f^2/N + (Dt + D_f^2/Dt) sigma/sqrt(N)) both deliver the canonical O(1/sqrt(N)) constant-stepsize rate. Same scaling, same stepsize choice motif (theta/(sigma sqrt(N))-style); paper A measures E[f-f*], paper B measures E||grad f||^2/L.
Paper A's mirror descent SA efficiency theorem has no counterpart in paper B (no mirror-descent / non-Euclidean machinery in paper B).

Both establish high-probability / large-deviation refinements under a light-tail (sub-Gaussian) noise assumption: paper A's Proposition 2.2 gives Prob{f(x_avg)-f* > c/sqrt(N) (12+2 Omega)} <= 2 exp(-Omega); paper B's Corollary 2 gives a sub-Gaussian high-probability bound on ||grad f(x_bar*)||^2 with the third-order Lambda dependence eliminated. Same role (sharpening tail bounds via light-tail), different output target.

Both are high-probability complexity theorems for two-phase / robust schemes: paper A's Proposition 3.2 bounds Prob{epsilon_phi(x_avg) > ...} for the mirror saddle-point algorithm; paper B's Theorem 2 gives Prob{||grad f(x_bar*)||^2 >= ...} <= (S+1)/lambda + 2^{-S} for 2-RSG. Both pair the meta-algorithm with a light-tail or boosted Markov-style argument.
Paper A's saddle-point mirror SA efficiency theorem has no paper-B counterpart (paper B has no saddle-point setup).
Paper A's matrix-game refined large-deviation bound is specific to the bilinear matrix game setup, with no analogue in paper B.
Paper B's RSGF convergence theorem (zeroth-order analogue of Theorem 1) has no paper-A analogue.
Constant-stepsize complexity of RSGF — zeroth-order specific, no paper-A counterpart.
Convergence/complexity of 2-RSGF — zeroth-order two-phase, paper-B specific.

Paper A's prox-mapping inequality (Lemma 2.1) is the central technical lemma of the mirror-descent analysis. Paper B's analysis uses the smoothness inequality / descent lemma instead; no direct counterpart in paper B's paper-original lemmas.
Paper A's saddle-point error bound lemma is specific to the saddle-point mirror SA analysis; no paper-B counterpart.

Lemma 6.1 (telescoping prox-mapping bound) is a paper-A appendix lemma underlying the mirror-descent saddle-point analysis. No direct paper-B equivalent (paper B telescopes the smoothness inequality directly).

Both are sample-complexity discussion remarks. Paper A compares N_SA vs N_SAA scaling under light-tail; paper B's RP248.2 / RP248.3 discuss the improved 2-RSG complexity scaling (and its sub-Gaussian sharpening). Same flavor: refined complexity counting for the robust two-phase / averaged scheme.

Proof structure parallel: paper A's PP247.3 (proof of saddle-point error bound) and paper B's PP248.1 (proof of RSG / Theorem 1) follow the same blueprint — apply per-step bound, telescope, take expectation killing martingale cross-terms via the iid noise assumption, conclude via choice of weights. Paper A uses Lemma 2.1 (prox-mapping) as the per-step bound; paper B uses the smoothness inequality. Composite L1-L1 match; the inner step DAGs differ (PSP247.1-5 vs PSP248.1-6) but encode the same sequence of moves.

Composite L2 cluster correspondence accompanying the parent proof match above. Both step sequences follow: (i) apply per-iteration bound (prox lemma vs smoothness lemma), (ii) introduce noise term Delta_t = G - g, (iii) telescope/sum, (iv) take expectation using martingale property and bounded second moment, (v) conclude via stepsize-weighted aggregation. The per-step subclass tags align (apply_lemma -> apply_lemma; introduce_variable / algebraic_manipulation -> algebraic_manipulation; bound_estimate -> bound_estimate; conclude -> conclude). Low confidence reflects different objectives (saddle-gap vs gradient-norm) and that paper A's proof targets Lemma 3.1, not the analog of paper B's Theorem 1.

Both are constant-stepsize-substitution proofs: paper A's proof of Proposition 2.2 is delegated to adapting Proposition 3.2's argument with bound (2.39); paper B's proof of Corollary 1 substitutes gamma_k = min{1/L, Dt/(sigma sqrt(N))} into Theorem 1. Same routine plug-in role.

Proof structure parallel: paper A's PP247.4 (Prop 3.2) decomposes into deterministic-stochastic + martingale parts and applies Markov + Cramer/Azuma; paper B's PP248.3 (Theorem 2 / 2-RSG) decomposes into a three-term split, bounds min over independent runs by 2^{-S}, and bounds noise via the Juditsky-Nemirovski martingale lemma. Same overall template (decompose, bound each piece, calibrate the failure probability to Lambda).

Composite L2 cluster: both inner DAGs perform a decomposition + bounding + calibration sequence for the high-probability theorem. The objects bounded differ (saddle-gap martingale vs three-term gradient-norm split with min over S runs), but the template (split / lemma application / aggregate / set lambda) lines up. Low confidence because paper A's PSP247.1-5 belong to the saddle-point Lemma 3.1 proof, not directly the high-probability Prop 3.2 proof; the strongest analog for paper B's PP248.3 inner steps is the (unextracted) inner step DAG of paper A's PP247.4.

Paper A cites Polyak-Juditsky averaging as the asymptotic-optimality result motivating robust averaged SA. Paper B's RSG randomization is a parallel device targeting the same robustness property in the nonconvex regime. Cited prior work in A vs paper-original contribution in B — meaningful for relation_type EXT.

Robbins-Monro SA (cited foundational scheme in paper A) is the common ancestor of both papers' algorithms; paper B's RSG inherits the SGD recurrence directly from this lineage. External-origin in A maps to paper-origin contribution in B.

Paper A's cited Azuma-Hoeffding (used in proof of Prop 3.3) and paper B's cited Juditsky-Nemirovski vector-valued martingale large-deviation lemma (used in proofs of Theorem 2 and Corollary 2) play the same role: martingale concentration tool for converting expected bounds into high-probability bounds. Paper B's lemma is the vector-valued generalization; both are external citations in their respective papers.
SAA (sample average approximation) cited in paper A as the alternative methodology compared against SA. Not used in paper B.

Paper A's saddle-point, minimax, and matrix-game problem variants extend the core stochastic optimization problem in directions orthogonal to paper B's nonconvex-smooth direction. No paper-B counterparts.
Saddle-point oracle assumption (A'2) — paper-A specific.
